senses.d: By or for the cause that; on this account that; for the reason that.
ex: I hid myself because I was afraid.

senses.d: As is known, inferred, or determined from the fact that.
ex: It must be broken, because I pressed the button and nothing happened.
I don't think he is a nice person, because he yells at people for no reason.
Simon[…]set the house on fire where he was born, because nobody should point at it.
My life is ruined because of you!
And God blessed the seuenth day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his worke, which God created and made.

senses.d: Used alone to refuse to provide a full answer to a question begun with "why", usually taken as an anapodoton of the elided full phrase "Because I said so".

ex: He rejected me because revenge, I guess.
It doesn't work because reasons.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French par cel que (literally “by this that”). Cognates with Catalan perquè; Italian perché; Portuguese and Spanish porque.
From Old French quer (“as, since, because, for”), from Latin quārē (“how; why”). Compare Catalan car.
Compare à cause de.

Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

Cognate with Spanish ya que and Italian giacché.

ety.text: A compound of the sources of be- + come. From Middle English becomen, bicumen, from Old English becuman (“to come (to), approach, arrive, enter, meet with, fall in with; happen, befall; befit”), from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną (“to come around, come about, come across, come by”), equivalent to be- (“about, around”) + come.

senses.d: begin to be; turn into (often with permanent states).
ex: Near-synonyms: get, turn, go, come, fall, grow, wax
She became a doctor when she was 25.

senses.d: To come about; happen; come into being; arise.
ex: What became of him after he was let go?
It hath becomen so that many a man had to sterve.
It doesn’t become a true gentleman to speak in such a manner.

Ay, lord, she will become thy bed, I warrant,
And bring thee forth brave brood.

senses.d: Of an adornment, piece of clothing etc.: to look attractive on (someone).
ex: That dress really becomes you.
But, madam, where is Warwick then become?
Hallo, this is my favorite URL. You can surfing and become cash.^([sic])

ety.text: From Middle English bek, bekk, becc, from Old English bæc, bec, bæċe, beċe (“beck, brook”), from Proto-Germanic *bakiz (“stream”). Cognate with Old Norse bekkr (“a stream or brook”), Low German bek, beck, German Bach, Dutch beek, Swedish bäck, Doublet of batch. More at beach.

From Middle English bekken, a shortened form of Middle English bekenen, from Old English bēcnan, bēacnian (“to signify; beckon”), from Proto-West Germanic *baukn, from Proto-Germanic *baukną (“beacon”). More at beacon.
See back.

ex: […]Whence, climing to the Cleeves, her selfe she firmlie sets / The Bourns, the Brooks, the Becks, the Rills, the Rivilets[…]
